title: Fighting for Your Light: Anusia Gillespie on AI, Legal Innovation, and the Soul Toll of Law
author: Anusia Gillespie

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Gillespie’s systems thinking and broad commitment to legal innovation are compatible with redesigning legal delivery, but the excerpt does not address AI-driven pricing pressure, buyer incentives, verification, staffing structures or apprenticeship. It therefore provides too little evidence to establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The supplied excerpts are closing remarks limited to Gillespie’s role, novel, contact details and purchase information. They provide no substantive claim about organisational adaptation, human control, employment, preparation, pricing or AI adoption architecture, so her position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that automation requires deliberate organisational development rather than simple task substitution, and materially extends the cluster by identifying billable-hour habits as a cultural barrier requiring firm-wide training and change management. It does not directly establish effects on apprenticeship or partner succession.
qs: And the single most important thing to prepare people for what’s coming is to solve for this impediment to innovation and collaboration, adaptability, agility, and make it as part of that initiative, like really widely known and trained on in the firm as to why they’re doing that and what’s expected.
It’s a huge change management effort, but that’s what I think has to be done.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: Shaver directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that procurement and rollout do not themselves produce realized value. She identifies a substantial gap between firm-wide deployment and adoption, and argues that workflow limitations, lawyer training and deliberate adoption methods remain necessary.
qs: So recent studies have indicated that although approximately 70 % of the AmLaw 100  firms have rolled out some form of generative AI firm-wide, adoption rates of that technology hover around 25%.
Adoption really still is an issue and firms are grappling with it and methodologies that can help to drive adoption are really still necessary.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Gillespie supports the cluster’s emphasis on selective, network-based learning rather than indiscriminately following releases or media narratives. Her internal knowledge-sharing channels and conversations with legal-innovation peers provide contextual filtering, though her account is anecdotal rather than empirical validation.
qs: I’m quite fortunate at VLex to have internal channels, including a competitive intelligence channel where some of the best minds in the world and legal are constantly sharing.
And it’s just like the watering hole of reality versus the hype of the media.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Gillespie directly supports the cluster’s view that legal-AI innovation is an organisational change challenge shaped by incentives and ingrained professional habits, not merely a technology purchase. She identifies the billable-hour mindset as a barrier to experimentation and calls for firm-wide communication, training and change management.
qs: if the thought process with a lawyer is always, how do I shorten this conversation so that I can get back to my billable hours, just like on repeat, then not much is going to get done beyond doing the same thing that we’ve always done.
It’s a huge change management effort, but that’s what I think has to be done.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that purchasing or deploying legal AI does not ensure effective use. It distinguishes rollout from adoption and argues that lawyers need training and firms need deliberate adoption methodologies. Its cited adoption figures are qualified and methodologically unspecified, consistent with the cluster’s caution about treating deployment and actual use as equivalent measures.
qs: So recent studies have indicated that although approximately 70 % of the AmLaw 100  firms have rolled out some form of generative AI firm-wide, adoption rates of that technology hover around 25%.
Adoption really still is an issue and firms are grappling with it and methodologies that can help to drive adoption are really still necessary.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Gillespie supports the cluster’s principal work-redesign proposition by welcoming the transfer of routine legal drudgery to machines so lawyers can focus on higher-level, mission- and people-centred work. Her account is experiential and does not substantively address jagged capability, verification or implementation evidence, so it supports rather than materially extends the synthesis.
qs: ⁓ Second is that my day job is in legal technology and we are putting more and more of the drudgery of being a lawyer into machines and that’s a really good thing.

It’s a systemic improvement that better positions lawyers to do higher brow work and connect to the mission and people of that work in doing so and so that’s kind of creating more room for soul, more room for all of these other pieces and that’s how it all comes together.

kp.k: Resistance can become an opportunity for technology adoption
kp.d: Gillespie argues that negative reactions from lawyers, including powerful partners, can signal engagement rather than failure. She distinguishes this from exposing lawyers prematurely to tools that produce poor experiences. As anecdotal support, she describes a frustrated lateral litigation partner at Stradley who, with support during a vLex curriculum initiative, completed client work within a week or two, attended a baseball game that evening, received positive client feedback, and became a champion. This is her account of a customer experience, not measured adoption evidence.
qs: It means I have their attention, whether it’s a positive or a negative reaction.
Whereas if you say, well, wait, let’s just lean into that more and use that energy to bring that person around and be our biggest champion, that’s an opportunity.
then within a week or two, he found a client use and got a piece of work product done that literally allowed him to go to a baseball game that night.

kp.k: Legal career systems can constrain individual agency
kp.d: Gillespie connects her interest in systemic reform to her experience as a commercial real estate associate: developing business offered career agency, but bank relationships were already allocated, leaving inherited accounts as the route to business development. She uses her novel's fictional protagonist to illustrate a broader critique of predefined success, incentives and constraints that keep lawyers pursuing the next career rung. The fictional illustration is a framework for her argument, not empirical evidence about the profession.
qs: as a law firm associate, I knew that the only way to get agency in your career is to develop business.
So the only way to develop business was to be handed down accounts. It was all part of this system.
she was placed on a track within law with a predefined definition of success and with incentives and constraints that keep her there chasing the next rung.

kp.k: Automating drudgery could support more meaningful legal work
kp.d: Gillespie presents transferring routine legal drudgery to machines as a systemic improvement that better positions lawyers for higher-level work and connection with clients and professional purpose. She links this to her 'soul toll' framework: monitoring the balance between meaningful work and its personal costs. This is a qualitative argument about technology's potential and professional well-being, without quantified productivity or health outcomes.
qs: what’s your ratio of soul and toll in your work, in your life, holistically?
First, we want lawyers to be healthy, high-performing athletes to contribute their highest and best to the legal operating system of the world.
we are putting more and more of the drudgery of being a lawyer into machines and that’s a really good thing.
It’s a systemic improvement that better positions lawyers to do higher brow work and connect to the mission and people of that work in doing so

kp.k: Generative immediacy changes lawyers' enthusiasm for technology
kp.d: Responding to Lambert's observation of renewed energy in technology discussions with attorneys, Gillespie says she shares that impression. She contrasts generative technology's immediate experience with process mapping and automation, which lawyers may find less engaging even when the eventual output is attractive. Both speakers offer practitioner impressions rather than systematic evidence.
qs: I feel it too. I think that moving from process and automation to something generative and immediate is just a whole different ball game that is much more exciting.
Lawyers are not steeped necessarily in process mapping. Automation wasn’t necessarily going to be such an exciting process to go through. Maybe the output of it.

kp.k: Billable-hour thinking impedes innovation and collaboration
kp.d: Gillespie identifies the billable hour as the profession's biggest impediment to change, emphasizing its effect on attention and mindset rather than explicitly proposing a replacement pricing model. She argues that pressure to return to billable work crowds out innovation, collaboration, adaptability and agility. She recommends addressing this impediment through a firm-wide change-management initiative that explains its purpose and expectations. Her personal illustration is that stopping six-minute-increment thinking took a full year after less than two years of practice.
qs: I think the biggest impediment to change in the legal profession is the billable hour.

if the thought process with a lawyer is always, how do I shorten this conversation so that I can get back to my billable hours, just like on repeat, then not much is going to get done beyond doing the same thing that we’ve always done.
It took me a full year to stop thinking in six minute increments and I only practiced for less than two years.
like really widely known and trained on in the firm as to why they’re doing that and what’s expected.

kp.k: Technology adoption duties differ from duties to innovate
kp.d: Asked whether professional competence should evolve and whether reclaimed time creates an ethical duty to emphasize human aspects of practice, Gillespie instead distinguishes a duty to innovate from a duty to keep pace with relevant technology. Reasoning from consumer protection for uninformed buyers using solo lawyers, she supports an affirmative responsibility to adopt relevant new technologies and argues it should apply across lawyers. She explicitly remains uncertain about the relative roles of ethics and market forces; she does not identify an existing professional rule imposing this duty.
qs: I struggle is how much of this is ethics and how much is market forces that shapes how this plays out?
And is it an ethical duty to innovate?
or an ethical duty to keep pace with and adopt technology. And I view those as different things.
If I’m protecting the consumer in that instance, then yes, I think a lawyer should have an affirmative responsibility to keep pace with and adopt relevant new technologies.
And you can’t create those kind of duties just for one type of lawyer versus another type of lawyer. So then I think it has to be across the board.

kp.k: Client capabilities and competition pressure firms to adopt
kp.d: Gillespie describes clients' own adoption and understanding of AI tools as a source of pressure on law firms' service delivery, including technology questions in RFPs. She also identifies consolidation and competitive pressure among mid-sized firms as adoption drivers. These are asserted market mechanisms, with no named transactions, adoption measurements or client sample provided.
qs: Yeah, by market forces, I mean clients adopting these tools themselves and knowing what they can do and then pushing back on law firms and the way that they’re delivering services in RFPs, asking what technologies you’re using and providing a lot of pressure that way.
market forces and consolidation in kind mid-sized law firms that must adopt this technology to compete.

kp.k: Continuous technological change requires deliberate recovery boundaries
kp.d: In the forward-looking discussion, Gillespie predicts that technological change will not provide the pause some legal innovation professionals expect. She warns conditionally that without self-created recovery time and real boundaries, people may burn out and leave quickly. Her practical recommendations include restricting commitments to three agreed priority areas and taking ten minutes for self-reflection. These are personal recommendations and a forecast, not measured AI-related attrition or clinical findings.
qs: I kept hearing people say, when this slows down, then I’m going to take a break.
This isn’t going to slow down.

so when there’s no natural pause anymore, people are going to have to create that for themselves and set new real boundaries. Or I think on the human side, we’re going to see a lot of people burn out and drop out really fast.
And if it doesn’t fit into one of those three buckets, then it’s a no.
You can just sit with yourself for 10 minutes and see what that’s like.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shaver says firm-wide availability of generative AI does not ensure adoption, and chat interfaces require training and are poorly suited to legal workflows.
pts.d: In the introductory resource segment (00:14), Nikki Shaver distinguishes rolling out technology from lawyers actually using it. She reports approximately 70% firm-wide rollout among AmLaw 100 firms versus adoption around 25%, citing unspecified recent studies. She argues that adoption programs remain necessary.

pts.k: Gillespie argues that resistance to legal technology can become advocacy through targeted support.
pts.d: At 06:46, Anusia Gillespie describes a frustrated lateral litigation partner becoming a champion after assistance revealed a useful client application. Her claim concerns engagement and adoption, not the desirability of releasing immature tools.

pts.k: Gillespie says machines can reduce legal drudgery and create room for higher-level, more meaningful work; generative technology also produces greater excitement than process automation.
pts.d: At 12:54 and 14:40, Gillespie frames technology as augmenting lawyers by freeing capacity for substantive work and connection with people and professional purpose. She describes increased excitement as her own observation, rather than a measured workforce outcome.

pts.k: Gillespie identifies the billable-hour mindset as a major impediment to technological change.
pts.d: At 18:12–18:38, Gillespie argues that pressure to return immediately to billable work obstructs innovation, collaboration and adaptability. She recommends addressing that mindset through a substantial, clearly explained and trained change-management initiative; she does not specify a replacement pricing model.

pts.k: Gillespie advocates a responsibility to adopt relevant technologies and says informed clients and competition already pressure firms to do so.
pts.d: At 20:32–21:43, Gillespie distinguishes a duty to innovate from a duty to keep pace with technology. Her proposed affirmative responsibility is a normative position, not a statement of an established professional rule. Separately, she says clients using the tools themselves challenge service delivery and ask about technology in RFPs, while consolidation and competition pressure mid-sized firms.

pts.k: Gillespie predicts continued rapid technological change and fast burnout or departure unless people deliberately establish pauses and boundaries.
pts.d: At 23:31–23:57, Gillespie rejects the expectation of an imminent slowdown. Her prediction connects sustained technological demands with human sustainability, rather than predicting AI-driven job substitution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The adoption figures are attributed to unnamed studies; the principal interview claims rely on professional experience, anecdotes and argument.
pts.d: Shaver supplies no study titles, methods, dates or precise denominator for the approximately 25% adoption rate. Gillespie's adoption example is a single partner's reported time saving and positive client response, not a controlled productivity or quality study. Her account of the billable-hour mindset draws on personal experience. She mentions earlier interviews with experts when discussing ethical obligations, but does not provide their findings or attribute her position to them. The pace and burnout prediction follows conference observations and her experience of the preceding three years. No model benchmarks or measured burnout outcomes are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims concern current adoption and an open-ended near future, with benefits dependent on training, relevant uses, organizational change and personal boundaries.
pts.d: In this 2025 source, Shaver describes recent adoption conditions and variation across firms. Gillespie's partner anecdote concerns a conversion to advocacy within one or two weeks after she predicted three weeks, conditional on invested support. She excludes premature introductions that create poor experiences. The proposed technology responsibility concerns relevant technologies and begins with consumer protection; organizational market pressure is presented more tentatively for larger entities. The burnout prediction has no numerical horizon or forecast rate and is conditional on failing to create recovery time.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include lawyers adopting AI, firm leaders, legal AI buyers, solo clients, larger organizational clients and mid-sized firms facing competition.
pts.d: Shaver specifically discusses AmLaw 100 rollout and adoption resources for firms and other legal AI buyers. Gillespie's example involves a lateral litigation partner at the firm identified in the transcript as Stradley; reduced work time benefits his personal life while serving a client. Her broader augmentation claim concerns lawyers' work quality, meaning and well-being. Leaders must address billable-hour incentives. Solo lawyers and uninformed buyers motivate her consumer-protection argument, which she extends across the profession. Clients with their own AI experience exert purchasing pressure, and mid-sized firms face competitive adoption demands. The burnout warning concerns people sustaining the pace of legal technological change.
